# Watch People Die Live

> A real-time statistical mortality globe. Every flash on the globe is one modelled death, placed
> on a population-density grid weighted by that country's death rate. The people are
> representative personas assembled from public demographic data — not records of identifiable
> individuals, and not reports of deaths that have happened.

The site is a single scrolling data story with a live 3D globe at the top. It explains how the
model is built, in this order: **Where** a death is placed (global rate, then country rate, then
sub-national region), **When** it happens (seasonality, and the search for a usable proxy for it),
**Who** it happens to (age, sex, cause), conflict deaths, and what the model still gets wrong.

Published in English, Catalan and German. The language is chosen by a `?lang=` query parameter:
`/` (English), `/?lang=ca`, `/?lang=de`. All three are the same story and the same figures.

## Pages

- [The story, in English](https://watchpeopledie.live/): the globe and the full explanation.
- [La història, en català](https://watchpeopledie.live/?lang=ca)
- [Die Geschichte, auf Deutsch](https://watchpeopledie.live/?lang=de)

## What the data is

- Crude death rate by country: World Bank.
- Population density: a baked grid, joined to country death rates offline. The globe samples the
  combined grid at runtime rather than computing the join in the browser.
- Deaths by age, sex and cause: UN Data Portal and WHO cause-of-death shares.
- Seasonality: sub-national monthly mortality where it exists, with a climate-zone fallback where
  it does not.
- Conflict deaths: ACLED.

## Please read before citing

Every persona is synthetic. The globe does not know that anyone in particular has died; it draws
from rates. A flash means "a death of roughly this kind is statistically due about now, somewhere
in this region", and nothing more specific than that. Numbers on the page are modelled estimates,
not counts, and should be attributed to the model rather than to the underlying sources.
